NPS, the urea units have been placed in six groups based on vintage and 
feedstock, for determining the group based concession rates. These groups are: 
pre-1992 gas based units, post-1992 ga s based units, pre-1992 naphtha based 
units, post-1992 naphtha based units, Fuel Oil/ Low Sulphur Heavy Stock 
(FO/LSHS) based units and mixed energy based units.The group based concession 
rates w.e.f. 1.4.2003 would be computed on the basis of the retention prices 
applicable as on 1.4.2002 duly updated for escalation/de-escalation in respect of 
feedstock, fuel, purchased power and water for the year 2002-03. 
Subsidy on decontrolled phosphatic and potassic fertilizers is given under 
the Concession Scheme. The concession rates for di-ammonium phosphate 
(DAP) are worked out for all the manufacturers after adjusting the imported 
ammonia and imported phosphoric acid prices prevailing in the international 
market. Rates of concession for comple x fertilizers are worked out after 
adjusting the nutrients cost based on the raw materials, ammonia, urea, 
phosphoric acid prices prevailing in the international market and naphtha prices 
prevailing in the indigenous market. Manufacturers of single super phosphate 
(SSP) are provided subsidy uniformly at the rate of Rs. 650 per metric ton. 
(c) The NPS for urea and the methodology of calculating the rates of 
concession for decontrolled phosphatic and potassic. fertilizers have been 
adopted to ensure greater transparency, efficiency and uniformity and to allow 
fair price to the manufacturers/ suppliers of these fertilizers.

elementary education may elude the country even around 2015, five years

literacy target by 2015? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. SANJAY PASWAN): (a) to (c) 
UNESCO has brought out a EFA Global Monitoring Report, 2002 in which India 
has been shown at serious risk of missing the EFA goals of Universal Primary 
Education and Total Literacy by 2015. The conclusions drawn in this Report are 
based on data available to UNESCO on the parameters of net enrolment ratio in 
primary schools, gender parity as per gross enrolment ratio in primary schools and 
the percentage of audit literacy. The data used by UNESCO for these parameters 
were either outdated or not available to UNESCO as far as I ndia is concerned. 
Further, initiatives taken in the recent years like launch of Sarva Shiksha 
Abhiyan and restructuring of literacy programme have not been taken into 
account for arriving at the conclusions. 
120 

[25 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(d) The initiatives of the Government  for achieving the literacy target 
include:— 
(1) The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (S SA) to achieve universalization 
of elementary education. The objectives of SSA are : 
— All children in school, Education Guarantee Centre, Alternate School, 
'Back-to-School' camp by 2003 
— All children complete five years of primary schooling by 2007 
— All children complete eight years of elementary schooling by 2010 
— Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis 
on education for life 
— Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 2007 
and at elementary education level by 2010 
— Universal retention by 2010 
(2) The literacy schemes of the National Literacy Mission (NLM) 
have been restructured to achi eve continuity, efficiency and 
convergence in the implementation of the Literacy Campaigns and 
expansion in the scope of the Continuting Education programme. 
— NLM aims to achieve a sustainable threshold level of 75% 
literacy by 2007.

colleges 
632.    SHRI GAYA SINGH: 
SHRI N.R. DASARI: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the recent news 
reports about the sale of medical and engineering seats in unaided private 
colleges; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction to such 
uncontrolled trade in professional education field; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the private colleges have resorted to this 
practice misinterpreting a Supreme Court judgement of December, 2002 freeing 
unaided private colleges from Government fee control; and 
(d) if so, what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR.  VALLABHBHAI RAMJIBHAI 
KATHIRIA):(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (d) As per the judgement of Hon'ble Supreme Court dated 31st 
October, 2002 in the T.M.A. Pai Foundation & Others Versus State of 
Karnataka and Others Case, in professional un-aided institutions, a rational fee 
structure should be adopted by the Management, which would not be entitled to 
charge a capitation fee. Appropriate machinery can be devised by the State or 
University to ensure that no capitation fee is charged and that there is no 
profitering, though institutions may be permitted to accumulate a reasonable 
surplus for furtherance of education. Accordingly, an Interim Policy Regulation 
was notified by AICTE on 20th March, 2003, according to which, State 
Governments are to decide a fee structrue for the Institutions in the respective 
State for the academic year 2003-04. The Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare have also issued similar guidelines in respect of private medical 
colleges on 14th May, 2003. The matter is at present Sub-judice.

Load of school bags on children 
†652. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the load of school bags on children is increasing alongwith the 
load of studies;

increasing load of books on children; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. VALLABHBHAI RAMJIBHAI 
KATHIRIA): (a) to (c) The National Curriculum Framework for School 
Education-2000 has made recommendations aimed at reducing the total load,

Work Education and Health Education into the Art of

information would further reduce this burden upto the secondary level. 
South Indian languages in Hindi speaking states and UTs 
653. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government had introduced a scheme in 
1993-94 to teach a South Indian language in Hindi speaking States and UTs; 
(b) if so, the number of South Indian languages i.e. Telugu, Tamil, 
Kannada and Malayalam which were introduced, number of teachers 
appointed and the amount spent on each  language, since the inception of 
scheme, year-wise; 
(c) whether there is any plan to make one South Indian language 
compulsory in Hindi speaking States and UTs for the promotion of National 
integration through language; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR.  VALLABHBHAI RAMJIBHAI 
KATHIRIA): (a) and (b) The Government of India launched a Scheme called 
Appointment of Modern Indian Language Teachers (MIL) in 1993-94 with the 
objective of implementation of Three Language Formula and promoting 
national integration as well as to help the development of composite Hindi by 
drawing on from the regional languages as envisaged in the Constitution. 
Under the scheme a grant was releas ed to the Government of Haryana 
and to the Government of Himachal Pradesh in the year 1994-95.13 Tamil 
teachers had been appointed by the Government of Himachal Pradesh to teach 
Tamil in the schools of the State. In the 10th plan the scheme is being 
implemented under a wider scheme of Appointment of Language Teachers. 
154 

[25 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) and (d) All the schools affiliated to Council for the Indian School 
Certificate Examinations (CISCE) and Central Board of Secondary 
Education (CBSE) have already implemented Three Language Formula which 
includes the study of Hindi, English and a Modern Indian language, preferably 
one of the Southern languages in the Hindi speaking States and of the regional 
language Hindi and English in the non-Hindi speaking States for the promotion 
of National integration through languages.

Training and Supervision in Railways 
662. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 65 per cent of the causes of train accidents are 
attributed to human error; 
(b) whether this reflects a low standa rd of training and supervision in 
Railways; and 
(c) if so, what are Government views on this? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) NO, Sir. This does not reflect low standards of training on 
Railways. Indian Railways is a vast organization employing about 15.15 lakh 
staff and in the fact of safety considerations and manpower variety, training on 
the Railways is given a very high priority. All staff, including safety category 
staff, are properly trained before extensive utilization of newly acquired 
technological aids is adopted. Modifying and refreshing the training of 
Railway staff to update their knowledge and skill is a continuous process. A 
comprehensive training need analysis of all categories of staff is carried out 
and training modules are revised to suit the changes in technology, work 
practices and objectives of the job. Additional funds have also been allotted to 
the training centres for upgradation of training facilities. 
Ultrasonic Flaw Detection Test during Monsoon 
663. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is mandatory for Railways to periodically patrol and 
176 

[25 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
run checks, including 'Ultrasonic Flaw Detection Test", on the Railway tracks, 
particularly during monsoon seasons and areas prone to heavy rainfall, 
landslides and shifting of land; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Konk an Railway Corporation had not 
undertaken the regular checks, including netting of the vulnerable areas, 
resulting in the recent accident on the Karwar-Ratnagiri Sector; and 
(d) if so, what measures are being cont emplated to ensure compliance of 
safety exercises by the Railways for prevention of accidents? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) and (b) Patrolling of Railway Track is 
carried out in identified sections, in accordance with extant instructions which 
cover all seasons including monsoon. Ultrasonic Flaw Detection Test is 
carried out on rails on need based concept, unrelated to season. 
(c) No, Sir. Konkan Railway Corporation Ltd. had undertaken regular 
checks including netting of the vulner able areas. The site of accident 
was, however, not considered vulnerable by the Expert Committee. 
(d) Railways are continuously st riving to prevent accidents and 
measures, being taken for ensuring compliance, include training of staff, 
safety awareness campaign, safety drives, monsoon precautions includng. 
identification of vulnerable spots and monsoon patrolling.

Elimination of subsidy by OECD 
707. SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE : Will the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether OECD (Organisation of Economic Cooperation and 
Development) has proposed to eliminate all specific subsidy for the steel 
industries for curbing the market distortions in international trade in steel; 
(b) if so, what would be its impact on Indian steel industries; and 
(c) whether India has made any effort to ensure support of other steel 
exporting countries like Brazil, Egypt, etc; if so, what are their response? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI 
BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY) (a) At the initiative of the OECD c ountries 
with interest in international steel trade have been deliberating upon issues 
relating to effectiveness of existing multilateral disciplines on market 
distorting measures relevant for trade in the steel sector.The proponents of the 
OECD steel deliberations are of the view that subsidies and related government 
support have caused and are causing significant distortions in the steel markets 
and these will be required to be reduced and where possible eliminated. 
Elements of a possible Steel Subsidy Agreement are being discussed by the 
participating countries. 
(b) While remaining engaged in the negotiating process, India is 
primarily trying to preserve the special and differential treatment provisions 
available to the developing countries under the existing WTO Agreement on 
Subsidies and Countervailing Measures.These provisions enable India to provide 
crucial export incentives to the industry, and if these are preserved, there is 
not likely to be any significant impact on the Indian steel industry. 
(c) Yes, Sir. However, there is divergen ce in the core interests of Egypt, 
Brazil and India. While India has been essentially trying to preserve the flexibility 
to provide export incentives available under Acticle 27 of the WTO 
Agreement on Subsidies ana Countervailing Measures. Egypt's main interest is 
protecting its ability to provide assistance for re-structuring of the steel industry 
including its privatisation. Brazil's core interest lie in protecting their ability to 
provide assistance to correct deficiencies  in their financial markets and aid to 
disadvantaged regions.

(b) if so, the salient features of the proposed legislation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI 
BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) Yes, Sir. A proposal to enact "Buy Indian 
Act" is under consideration of the Government. However, it may be noted 
that the proposal was mooted at a time  when the domestic industry had been 
passing through a severe crisis caused by low price and poor demand. The 
situation has shown improvement since January 2002 with the price of steel 
products on an increase and a fair amount of stability having been achieved. 
(b) Some of the salient features of the proposed legislation are as 
follows: 
(i) Every public work or industry established or run with the aid or 
assistance of public funds shall procure its requirment of iron and steel 
material from indigenous manufacturers unless use of such material is: 
(a) to be made outside India,. (b) to be contrary to public interest of 
detrimental to the project, (c) not available indigenously in specified 
quality or within the required delivery schedule. 
(ii) Every contract for construction, modification, modernisation, 
installation, alteration or repairs or any public works or industrial 
establishment, which is being undertaken with assistance from the 
public fund should contain a provision that for the performance and 
execution of the job, the person responsible shall use only such un-
manufactured or manufactured iron and steel material which have 
been mined, produced or manufactured within the country unless it is 
impracticable for successful completion of the work.

requiring procurement of iron and steel material from sources outside the

714. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware th at our lackluster performance in 
international athletics meets is due to factors like lack of continuity of 
trianing, our coaches being handica pped because of lack of knowledge

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS (SHRI VIJAY GOEL): (a) According to information made 
available by the Amateur Athletic Federation of India, the performance of Indian 
athletes in International Athletic meets has not been lackluster. Infact, the 
performance of Indian Athletes in various international events has been 
encouraging. India won two medals (1 silver and 1 bronze) in Women Section 
in the Commonwealth Games held in Manchester in 2002, for the first time 
ever. 
Similarly, in the Busan Asian Games 2002 Indian athletes finished 2nd 
after China in athletic medal tally and won 7 Gold, 6 Silver and 4 bronze 
medals. Out of total 11 Gold Medals won by India in the Asian Games, 7 
Gold medals were won by athletes only and two athletes set new Asian Games 
records during the Games.

Championship held in Colombo in August, 2002, won 10 medals (1 Gold, 5 Silver 
& 4 Bronze). Similarly, Indian Junior Athletic teamwon 14 medals (2 Gold, 4 
Silver and 8 Bronze) in Asian Junior championship held at Bangkok in 
October, 2002. In World Junior Athletic championship held at Kingston (Jamaica) 
in July, 2002, one athlete won a bronze medal and the others two figured in the 
best 8.

following measures are being taken:

WADA Sanctions 
715. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY:  Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) in the wake of recent incidences  of dope cases involving Indian 
athletes/sportsmen in large numbers, what corrective steps have been taken by 
the Indian Olympic Association/Government; 
(b) whether India is a signatory to the World Anti-Doping Agency 
declaration and if so, whether Indi a has cleared its past and present 
membership dues to WADA; and 
(c) wheher it is a fact that WADA's sanctions against erring member 
country would deny the country the right to carry the National flag on Olypic 
ceremories and non-playing of National Anthem for the winning 
athlete/team? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS (SHRI VIJAY GOEL): (a) The Indian Olypic Associations and 
National Sports Federation are primarily the action taking authorities against 
sportspersons found guilty of a doping offence. However, the Government of 
India, through Sports Authority of India has made serious efforts to keep away 
sports persons from use of any kind of prohibited drugs. During the coaching 
camps, strict instructions have been i ssued to the coaches attached with the 
campers to educate and regularly counsel and players about the banned drugs. 
Apart from this,the sports medicine doctors at NS NIS< Patiala and other 
regional centres conduct lecture, wherev er camps are being held, to educate 
the players not to use any banned drugs . At the time of commencement of the 
camp, each player is being provided with documents and brochures about the 
banned substances.The list of banned drugs and placards for education of players 
are put in the rooms of campers. Rooms and belongings of players are also 
searched and checked at regular intervals to see that no banned drugs are used 
besides testing the urine samples of sports persons during 
227 

RAJYA  SABHA [25 July, 2003] 
the coaching camps at random. Sports persons who have been found positive 
for Dope are removed from the camp/S AI Schemes and action is initiated 
against their coaches also, if found guilty. The Govt, of India has stopped 
giving any assistance to sports persons found guilty of doping offence under 
its sports promotion and other schemes. The IOA and Nationai Sports 
Federations take action against guilty players as per their rules and the rules of 
the respective international federations. 
(b) The proposal regarding signing the World Anti-Doping Agency 
declaration is under active consid eration of the Govt, and once the 
Government approves the proposal, India would be signing the Copenhagen 
Declaration 2003 on Anti-Doping in Sports. India has already paid the first 
year's subscription to WADA and the dues for the year 2003 would be paid 
very soon after Government approval. 
(c) Information is being collected and will be laid on the table of House.

GOVERNMENT MOTION 
For consideration of progress of implementation of Part IX and Part IX-
A of Constitution (contd.) 
THE MINISTER OF ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS AND THE 
MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION 
(MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I rise to intervene 
briefly in the discussion on the review of ten years of implementation of Part 
IX-A of the Constitution relating to the urban local bodies. My Ministry, that is, the 
Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation Ministry, of which I am holding 
the additional charge, circulated a background note giving the present status of 
the implementation of Part IX-A of the Constitution as regards urban local 
bodies, that is, the Municipalities. We have circulated a background note 
where we have given some of the data, 
233 

RAJYA  SABHA [25 July, 2003] 
which are available from the States, with regard to the implementation of the 
various directions given in the Seventy-fourth Amendments which was 
implemented from 1st of June, 1993. 
Sir, I am thankful to the speakers who raised various issues yesterday with 
regard to the implementation of the provisions of Part IX-A of the 
Constitution. Most of the speakers dwelt basically on the Panchayats. but all 
those problems, which were highlighted, relating to the Panchayats like non-
implementation of provisions of Part-IX A devolution of power, financial 
viability of the local bodies, are also  applicable to the urban local bodies, that 
is, the Municipalities. Therefore, I am thankful to all the Members who have 
highlighted those areas and I am quite sure that we will be benefited by them. 
The main provisions of the Act, as regards the urban local bodies, are also given 
on pages 3 to 9 of the background note which we have circulated. Basically, we 
have highlighted 12 items which needed urgent implementation. Yesterday, a 
number of speakers highlighted various shortcomings about implementation 
with regard to the Panchayats. As I said, these are also applicable. Shri Venkaiah 
Naidu gave a very detailed and very brilliant analysis of various problems and 
also suggested remedy for overcoming these maladies. A number of other 
Members also highlighted various issues. I am quite sure, with that analysis and 
with those suggestions, we will be able to move forward. I personally am in 
entire agreement with what has been said both about the non-devolution of real 
powers to the local bodies as also the financial non-viability of all these 
institutions which causes problems so far as the implementation is concerned. I, 
therefore, feel that we need do a major surgery for the implementation of 
provisions. Minor tinkering and minor remedial measures will not help. 
So far as the Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation is 
concerned, we had tried to interact with the State Government. We have had a 
number of meetings. We had made a number of suggestions with regard to 
implementation. Unfortunately, both the real devolution of power and financial 
delegation have not found favour. In the Background Paper, we have indicated 
the response of various States in regard to various provisions. We have not 
been very successful. However, we continue to put in our efforts. The data 
pertaining to our success or failure has been given in Annexures 1 to 5 to the 
Background Paper. 
234 

[25 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair) 
During this period, the Tenth Finance Commission and the Eleventh 
Finance Commission have also made certain provisions to help the local bodies. 
The Tenth Finance Commission had given Rs. 1,000 corres and the Eleventh 
Finance Commission has given Rs. 2,000 crores. I agree that this sum is 
inadequate. But it is a beginning. Ultimately, this also has to find its way 
right down to the local bodies, which normally does not happen in all cases for 
some reason or the other. At the Central level, we have been trying to improve 
the functioning of the local bodies by making various suggestions. The 
Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation has nine such 
schemes which I would put across to the States. Some progress has already been 
made.These schemes are: 
(1) Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns, (IDSMT) 
(2) Infrastructure development in Mega Cities; (3) Accelerated Urban Water 
Supply Programme, (AUWSP); (4) Low Cost Sanitation Scheme for 
Liberation of Scavengers; (5) Swar najayanti Shahari Rojgaar Yojana, 
(SJSRY); (6) Shelter and Sanitation Facilities for the Footpath Dwellers 
in Urban Areas; (7) National Network of  Building Centres; (8) Additional 
Central Assistance to States for Slum Development—National slum 
Development Programme and (9) The Balmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana 
(VAMBAY). 
In conclusion, I would only like to say that from the Central 
Government side, we will continue to make efforts to see that the local and 
urban bodies function efficiently. Th ere are a number of problems and 
obstacles which had been adequately highlighted yesterday. I think it is time 
which all of us should try and make efforts. Although it is a State subject and 
the ultimate delegation has to be done by the State, but it is the responsibility of 
all of us here to do whatever possible we can do to see that this system functicns 
efficiently. I hope after today's debate in both the Houses, the State Govenrments 
would be encouraged to do further real devolution of power as well as financial 
delegation so that the system functions efficiently. 
Madam, I thank you for having given me this opportunity to highlight the 
viewpoint of the Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation.

Water scarcity in the country 
SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nomin ated): Madam, a recent World 
Water Development Report ranked India a lowly 133rd among 188 countries 
in terms of water availability and 120th among 122 in terms of water quality. 
Water scarcity in India is largely man made. It is the result of a 
shortsighted pricing policy for public water supply that encourages wasteful 
use of water and makes it difficult to raise resources for upkeep and 
expansion of the system. 
India has 2.45 per cent of the world's land and 4 per cent of its fresh water 
resources. India's annual precipitation, snowfall and rain, is 4,000 billion cubic 
metre. This translates into 1869 BCM of water in river of which barely is 
used. Thus 1179 BCM of water flows into the sea. Add 432 BCM of 
groundwater the real availability of water is 1122 BCM which is sufficient to 
meet the needs of water of this country. 
We had prepared Five Year Plans for solution of water problem but the 
projects are ill funded and not completed. As of 2001, 159 major projects, 251 
medium ones and 94 renovation works have been pending since the 1960s. 
Keeping in view, therefore, we need to create autonomous and 
decentralized organisations with signifi cant user participation for setting up, 
financing and managing individual irrigation and domestic water supply systems. 
I, therefore, urge the Government should consider to take concrete 
measures and implement that so that  the problem of water is removed 
immediately.

SHRI R. KAMRAJ (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I would like to bring it to the 
notice of the House that f ood articles in our countr y are being increasingly

it is consumed within the country, mainly by the agriculture sector. The pesticides 
are also put to use for controlling pests and for public healthcare. A crop, like 
cotton which is grown on around five per cent of our agricultural land, consumes 
around 54 per cent of the total pesticides. This indicates the intensity of abuse of 
pesticides on this crop. In certain parts, farmers are known to spray 25 to 30 
times, on an average, during the cotton-cropping season.Through various 
processes, like volatilization, chemical mob ility, absorption by soil and 
sediment, pesticide drifting, and so on, these pesticides end up in places other

pesticides in our country, which are banned in their own country.

Government official passes an electronic data that has been received in his 
official capacity. It is now being realized that there is an urgent need to legislate 
for the protection of individual privacy.

*101.  MISS MABEL REBELLO:†† 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Export-Import Bank of India has identified herbal and 
medicinal plants as an important sub-sector for enhancement of exports; 
(b) whether the current global demand of the herbal and medicinal plants 
is around 51,000 crores and whether it has released a booklet in this regard; 
and 
(c) Government's action plan for exploiting the situation to the 
maximum in the global market? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): (a) to (c).A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The global demand for medicinal plants was estimated to be valued 
over Rs. 4,700 crores or US $ 1 billion (US $ 1000 million) in 2001. (1US$ = 
Rs. 47/- approx.) (Source: PC-TAS, ITC/UNCTAD, Geneva, SITC Code 
2924 - Plants and parts of plants primarily used for pharmacy, perfumery and 
insecticides: fresh, dried, powdered). EXIM Bank brought out an Occasional 
Paper (No. 54) on 'Indian Medicinal

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2003] 
Plants—A Sector Study in 1997. The updated study is under finalisation and is 
expected to be released in August, 2003. 
(c) Government's action plan for exploiting the situation to the maximum 
in the global market is summarized below:- 
• The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine under the Ministry of 
Health & Family Welfare has recently introduced a promotional scheme, 
through National Medicinal Plants Board, providing incentives for 
commercial cultivation of medicinal plants, which can aid in their 
export. 
• There are several Government initiatives focused specifically on 
medicinal plants resources. The Mini stry of Health has a programme 
called 'Vanaspathi-van scheme' for encouraging forest departments to 
raise medicinal plants on degraded forestlands. The Department of 
Indian System of Medicine has also been promoting establishment of 
herbal gardens and development of agro-technology protocols for 
prioritized species. 
• The Ministry of Environment and Forests has been implementing a 
pioneering programme in peninsular India for conserving wild 
populations of inter and intra specific medicinal plant diversity of that 
region. 
• The Department of Biotechnology has established four cryo-
preservation gene banks for medicinal plants to conserve the. species. 
• The Indian Council for Agricultural Research has been implementing 
an All India coordinated programme for the cultivation of medicinal 
and aromatic plants. 
• The Department of Science and Technology, through the Council for 
Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), has initiated an R&D 
project on traditional medicine, for standardizing prioritized herbal 
products under internationally acceptable norms. 
• The Office of Director General Foreign Trade, Department of 
Commerce, has issued a Notification No. 3 dated 31st March 2003, 
according to which plant and plant portions obtained from the wild and 
their cultivated varieties, except for 29 species of

under CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered

Government Authorities. Even formulations made from the 29 
prohibited species are freely exportable. 
• A panel has been formed in the CHEMEXCIL, an autonomous Export 
Promotion Council setup by the Department of Commerce, for giving 
thrust to exports of Ayurveda and Herbal Medicine. Financial 
assistance to individual exporters of the industry is also being granted for 
participating in International Trade Fairs through its Marketing 
Development Assistance (MDA) Programme. In addition, through its 
Market Access Initiative Scheme, th e Department of Commerce is 
financing the conduct of market study and follow-up activities to 
promote exports.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION

Statement 
(a) to (c) A Task Force was constituted on 28.1.2003 comprising all 
stakeholders including broadcasters, MSOs, cable operators, Equipment 
Manufacturers and representatives of Consumer Groups to examine various 
issues related to implementation of CAS, and to make recommendations on 
inter alia, the size and cost of basic service tier of free-to-air channels. On the

taxes) as the maximum price of basic se rvice tier, consisting of not less than 
30 free-to-air channels of different genres of entertainment, news, sports, 
children's programmes and music. Additional free-to-air channels would also 
be available to subscribers within the maximum amount mentioned. 
While monitoring the preparedness for CAS & during discussions with 
the stakeholders Broadcasters, MSOs, Cable Operators, Consumer Groups, the 
primary focus was on ensuring that co nsumers did not face any problems of 
shutdown of channels due to shortage of STBs. One of the options postponed 
was that of 'Dual feed'. This proposal envisaged that the Cable Operators 
transmit signals of pay channels, simultaneously in unencrypted and in 
encrypted mode. However after discussion with Cable Operators/MSOs, this 
option was not found practicable. It was found more appropriate to 
commence the roll ou t from September 1, 2003, in a phased-zonal manner in 
three metros of Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and at one go in Chennai. The 
intervening period would be used to step up preparedness, to ensure the 
availability of adequate numbers of STBs and to build up consumer 
awareness.

based to attract expectant mothers fo r institutional delivery. There is no 
disincentive for those who do not register.

Desert Medical Research Centre's Report on Diabetes 
•111. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMA D KHAN (DURRU): Will the 
Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Desert medical Research Centre of ICMR has come to the 
conclusion that persons belonging to Reika Tribe, inhabitants of Jodhpur 
region of Rajasthan, never suffer from diabetes; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government propose to encourage diabetes prone people to 
adopt the life-style of Reika Tribesmen; and 
(d) if so the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (d) A joint pilot study has been conducted by 
S.P. Medical College, Bikaner and the ICMR's Desert medicine Research 
Centre, Jodhpur to determine the prevalence of diabetes and IGT (impaired 
glucose tolerance) in Raica Community taking camel Milk, Raica Community 
not taking camel milk and Non-Raica Community not taking camel milk, living 
in the same geographical and socio-economic c onditions. This was a 
community based cross-sectional study in villages including rural and semi-
urban part of Jodhpur (North West Rajasthan): These subjects were grouped 
according to their habit of drinking camel milk. 
The study revealed that the prevalen ce of diabetes was almost at 0% 
level in Raica Community taking camel milk and low (1.1%) in Raica 
Community not taking camel milk while 2.8% in Non Raica Community not 
taking camel milk, living in the same geographical and socio-economic 
condition. The study has concluded that camel milk consumption is important 
when post-prandial glucose measurements is taken into account but the 
significant difference between Raicas and Non-Raicas who did not consume 
camel milk is a pointer towards a possible genetic advantage lying with 
Raicas to handle glucose better. Further studies are, however, required to 
confirm that consumption of camel milk will actually reduce the incidence of 
diabetes mellitus.

Under the provisions of Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules

Governments. The State Governments are advised from time to time to

fake drugs moving in the inter-state commerce to provide and strengthen

labs, to ensure speedy analysis of  drug samples for which they are

facilities in their labs. The State Governments have also been advised 
to keep strict surveillance over the suspected dealers; collect survey 
samples under national Survey Qua lity Evaluation of Drugs (NSQED) 
programme; constitute/r eactivate state drug advisory committees in

cases etc. ______________________________________________________

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2003]. 
Government of India has taken the following initiatives to tackle the 
problem of spurious drugs:- 
(i) Detailed guidelines in respect of strategies required to be adopted for 
efficient surveillance over the movement of spurious drugs were given 
to States on November 17, 1999, to  ensure focused surveillance over 
manufacture and sale of spurious drugs. 
(ii) Issues concerning alleged sale of spurious drugs was taken up by 
Union Health Minister with Stat e Health Ministers in the 7th 
Conference of Central Council of Health (CCH) & FW held on 12-13 
July, 2001. CCH resolved that in order to address issues relating to the 
increasing reports of spurious dr ugs/counterfeit drugs, special 
attention requires to be given to monitor and unearth such illegal 
activities by constituting a separate intelligence-cum-legal cell in the 
respective drug control organization and in seeking cooperation of the 
pharma industry, trade as wel as the police. 
(iii) Department of health constitu ted a broad based Committee under the 
Chairmanship of DGHS in July, 2001 , to examine issues concerning 
the problem of spurious drugs. The observations and recommendations 
of this Committee have been circulated on. September 16, 2002 to all 
State Drug Controllers for their information and necessary action in 
the matter. 
(iv) Union Minister of Health and Fa mily Welfare had specifically written 
to all Chief Ministers on October 8, 2002 on the issue of spurious 
drugs, seeking their personal intervention to ensure that adequate 
measures are taken in each State to vigorously pursue the strategies 
needed to preclude any possibility of menace of spurious products so as 
to collectively ensure its total eradication. 
(v) A meeting of Health Ministers and Senior Officials of 13 major States 
of the country was convened by Union Minister of Health and Family 
Welfare on 12.11.2002 to ensure concerted action to check any 
possible movement of spurious drugs in the country and to involve all 
stake holders to fight this menace. Suggestions/ views which emerged 
out of discussion were forwarded on January 8,2003 to all the State 
Governments for their information

and necessary action. One of the recommendations which emerged as 
outcome of discussion, was enactment of an Act on the lines of "The 
Gujarat Prevention of Anti-social Activities Act, 1985 (RASA)" by 
the State Governments for deterrent action against offenders. 
(vi) In order to increase the number of drug samples tested in the country 
and to bring down the reporting time to less than a month as against 3 to 
6 months presently being taken by many laboratories, a 
comprehensive plan has been undertaken by Central Government 
under a capacity building project to be implemented with World Bank 
assistance. 
(vii) In order to ensure speedy information exchange and networking of all 
States and Central Drugs Contro l Offices and Laboratories, a 
computerization project has been undertaken by Central Government. 
(viii) A specialized training programme for drugs control officers of all State 
Governments responsible for keeping surveillance over possible 
movement of spurious drugs has been formulated and was conducted 
from 25 June, 2003, by Central Government in cooperation with 
FDA, Maharashtra at Mumbai. 
(ix) Government of India have constituted a Committee of experts on

Director General, Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) 
to undertake a comprehensive review  of the drugs regulatory system 
in the country including the problem of spurious and substandard 
drugs and recommend remedial, measures to deal with this problem 
effectively. The committee has held two meetings on 26.2.2003 and 
17.7.2003 to undertake focused examination of two distinct areas of its 
terms of reference. Consultations with number of eminent persons and 
stakeholders has also been undertaken.

pointed out that satisfactory resolution with respect to 
distortions in global agricultural trade is possible only if both 
domestic support and export subsidies were substantially 
reduced or eliminated in the developed countries. India strongly 
emphasized the highest priority that it would give to the food 
security and protection of its farmers. India also stressed the need 
for sufficient special and differential treatment provisions for 
 
 
                                              46

[28 July, 2003]                 RAJYA   SABHA 
developing countries, such as the use of special safeguard measures in case of 
surge in imports. 
In respect of non-agricultural products India has strongly advocated 
increased market access for products of  export interest to India such as 
textiles, leather goods. It also stressed the need for providing for 'less than full 
reciprocity' in the matter of reduction commitments. Expressing strong interest 
in the services' negotiations, India has asked for greater liberalization in the 
movement of natural persons. 
On the so-called Singapore issues, namely Trade and Investment; Trade 
and Competition Policy; Transparency in Government Procurement; and 
Trade Facilitation, views are still divergent on many of the key aspects. Greater 
clarity would be required before any decision on modalities could be 
considered. 
The negotiations are an on-going process and while India's position on 
these issues generally remain as stated above, it is fine tuned from time to 
time depending upon the progress in individual negotiations. With regard to 
preparations for the Cancun Ministerial Conference, India has been taking steps 
at bilateral, plurilateral and multilateral levels, both with developed and 
developing country partners aimed at resolution of all the development-related 
issues, such as TRIPS and Public Health; Special and Differential Treatment; 
and Implementation-related issues, on a priority basis so as to have a 
successful outcome at the Cancun Minist erial Conference. Further, domestic 
consultations with stakeholders including State Governments and Union 
Territories and experts, on issues under negotiations are regularly held. 
Consultations with the political parties are part of the on going domestic 
consultation process. 
(c) and (d) India has been holding discussions with major trading 
partners, including the European Union (EU), China, Brazil and Mexico from 
time to time, on issues of shared common interests in the ongoing 
negotiations under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture. Most developing 
countries, including India, China and Brazil, favour substantial reductions in all 
forms of trade-distorting domestic support and elimination of export subsides 
provided by developed countries. The EU Member States, in turn, are 
prepared to agree only to gradual reductions in domestic support and export 
subsidies. The Cairns Group (which includes Brazil) and the United States 
(US) have demanded 
47 

RAJYA  SABHA [28 July, 2003] 
substantial improvements in market  access with elimination of export 
subsidies and reduction in trade distorting support. India and many 
developing country Members, however, favour minimal tariff reductions by 
developing countries. In the negotiations  held so far, there has been no 
convergence of views among Members of the WTO on many key issues.

738. SHRI CHO S. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many developing countries including India are 
opening up the farm sector under pressure from the WTO and IMF; 
(b) if so, its implications on the farm sector; 
(c) the steps being taken to protect that local farm sector from the 
unprincipled competition; and 
(d) whether Government are coming up with any new farm policy and if 
so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) and (d) India's commitments under the Agreement on Agriculture of the 
World Trade Organisation (WTO) have, by and large, not limited domestic 
policy options for the agriculture sector in India. Due to adverse balance of 
payments reasons, India was able to maintain quantitative restrictions on 
imports of agricultural products, and offer ceiling bindings of 100% for primary 
agricultural products, of 150% for processed agricultural products, and of 
300% for certain edible oils. With respect to domestic support commitments, 
the quantum of subsidies extended to farmers remains within the de minimis 
limit for developing countries, and India has, therefore, not had to undertake 
any reductions in the same. With regard to export subsidies also no reduction 
commitments were required to be undertaken, besides which India has the 
flexibility to provide export subsidies to reduce the marketing costs of exports 
of agricultural products and costs re lated to international and internal 
transport and freight charges on export shipments. 
With improvements in the balance of payments, the legal basis for 
maintaining quantitative restrictions on imports of agricultural products does 
not exist, and these restrictions have been phased out. However, in order to 
safeguard the domestic sector from any adverse impact, the Government is 
continuously monitoring the import of sensitive 
76 

[28 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
commodities and has put in place a suita ble mechanism for giving adeuqate 
protection to domestic producers through calibration of applied tariffs within the 
bound levels, and imposition of anti-dumping, anti-subsidy countervailing 
duty or safeguard action in accordance with relevant rules and disciplines of 
the WTO. Simultaneously, the Government provides support to Indian 
farmers by way of price support schemes, and various types of assistance under 
production programmes for different crops. 
In the on-going negotiations in agriculture in the WTO, India along with 
other WTO Members with similar interests and concerns have sought 
fundamental reform of the agriculture sector in developed countries through 
substantial reduction in trade-distortin g domestic support and elimination of 
export subsidies by them. India has also  indicated that adequate safeguards 
for domestic farmers must be provided in order to address situations of 
international price volatility and import surges. The negotiations are 
scheduled to be concluded by 1 January, 2005. 
The Government reviews its farm policy from time to time depending upon 
the exigencies of the situation and international developments.

process of objectively stru ctural clinical examinati on in the country for the

improve the patient care in the long run.

TB patients 
761. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will th e Minister of HEALTH AND-
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of people in the country affected by TB; 
(b) the steps taken by Government to check/eradicate this disease; 
(c) the causes for the spread of this disease; and 
(d) the number of human lives lost b ecause of TB annually during the 
last three years, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) It is estimated that about 22 lac 
new TB cases are occurring every year in the country. 
(b) To control the disease, National TB Control Programme is in 
operation in the country since 1962. This could not achieve the desired results. 
Therefore, Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) widely known 
as DOTS, which is a WHO recommended strategy, is being implemented in a 
phased manner, with the objective of achieving cure rate of 85% of new 
sputum positive cases. Diagnosis by sputum microscopy instead of by X-ray 
helps in detecting and curing infecti ous cases on priority. Facilities for 
diagnosis by sputum micr oscopy have been decentralized and strengthened. 
Drugs are provided under observation and patients are monitored so that they 
complete their treatment. Drugs are pr ovided free of cost in patient-wise 
boxes. 
The project districts have  reported a cure rate of more than 80% which 
means more than 8 out of every 10 patients diagnosed and put on treatment 
under revised strategy are successfully treated. This is double that of the earlier 
programme. 
To make the programme more accessi ble to larger segments of the 
population, and to supplement the Government efforts in this directions, 
emphasis is being given to also involve medical colleges, all general 
hospitals, private practitioners and NGOs in the programme. 
DOTS coverage is being rapidly expanded in the country. From 20 million 
coverage in 1998, about 700 million population has been covered at present. It is 
envisaged to cover 850 million population by 2004 under 
100 

[28 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
the revised strategy and the entire population of the country by 2005. 
(c) TB is an infectious disease.  It spreads through air and gets 
transmitted by inhalation of infected droplet nuclei which are discharged 
in the air when untreated sputum po sitive TB patient coughs or sneezes. 
Other contributory factors are poor housing conditions, overcrowding, 
illiteracy, under nutrition, lack of awareness of cause of illness among 
TB patients etc. All these factors are interrelated and contribute to the 
occurrence and spread of Tuberculosis. 
(d) Deaths are not reported under the National TB Control 
Programme. It is estimated that about  4.5 lac patients die of TB every 
year in the country. Under Revised National TB Control Programme 
(RNTCP), the deaths due to TB reported during the last three years are 
given in the enclosed Statement.

Statement 
Steps taken by the Government for prevention and control of dreaded 
diseases such as AIDS, Hepatitis, Cancer etc. 
(i) AIDS 
In order to prevent and control of HIV/AIDS, a comprehensive 
Programme is currently under implementation throughout the country 
as a 100% centrally sponsored scheme. The main components of the 
programme consist of:— 
* Preventive interventions for high risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer 
counselling and behaviour change communication. 
* Preventive interventions for the general population through 
programmes for blood safety, voluntary counselling and testing 
services, Information Education and Communication (IEC) and 
awareness building among adolescents. 
* Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure. 
* Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including interventions and public-private partnerships.. 
* Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through surveillance, training, monitoring and 
evaluation, technical resource gr oups, operational research and 
programme management. 
(ii) Hepatitis — A, B & C 
Hepatitis-A:-lt is a water borne disease and is spread through faeco-oral 
route. Vaccine for prevention of Hepatitis-A is not indige nously 
produced but is commercially available in the market. As Hepatitis-A is 
spread through contaminated water, the important prevention and control 
measures are supply of safe drinking water and sanitation in all areas. 
Hepatitis-B:-lt is spread through unsafe sex, unsafe blood 
109 

RAJYA  SABHA [28 July, 2003] 
transfusion, unsafe injections etc. and from mother to child. This is 
preventable by ensuring safe blood transfusion, safe sex, safe injection 
practices etc. Vaccine for Hepatitis - B is available. The following 
measures have been taken to prevent Hepatitis-B:— 
* Central Government Hospital personnel at high risk are being 
immunized against Hepatitis-B. State Governments have also been 
advised to take similar steps. 
* Guidelines have been issued for mandatory testing of blood in all' blood 
banks. 
* Promotion of safe sex under National AIDS Control Programme is 
advocated. 
* Health Awareness Campaigns under National AIDS Control 
Programme are held. 
* Guidelines have been issued to State Health Authorities for use of 
separate sterile syringes and needles for each injection. 
* A Pilot Project to immunize children against Hepatitis-B in selected 
Cities/Districts have been la unched under National Immunization 
Programme by Deptt. of Family Welfare. 
Hepatitis-C.—It is spread through unsa fe sex, unsafe blood transfusion, 
unsafe injections etc. and from mother  to child. This is preventable by 
ensuring safe blood transfusion, safe  sex, safe injection practices etc. 
Vaccine for Hepatitis-C is not available. The following measures have 
been taken to prevent Hepatitis-C:— 
* Mandatory testing of blood in all blood banks. 
* Promotion of safe sex under National AIDS Control Programme is 
advocated. 
* Health Awareness campaigns under National AIDS Control 
Programme are held. 
* Guidelines have been issued to State Health Authorities for use of 
separate sterile syringes and needles for each injection. 
110 

[28 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(iii) Cancer 
Under National Cancer Programme, there are 19 Regional Cancer Centres 
that are providing comprehensive cancer treatment to the patients and 
conducting research activities. Government of India is providing 
assistance under various schemes of National Cancer Control 
Programme to Medical Colleges/NG Os and State Governments for 
purchase of Cobalt Unit, Linear A ccelerator etc. and for conducting 
awareness and early detection activities on cancer.

Maternal mortality 
777. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: W ill the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that in country for every one lac 
pregnant females, 407 fall victim to maternal mortality, while worldwide one 
lac women die annually and another six lac become disabled; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
122 

[28 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, whether Government funded organizations, especially in 
villages have competent doctors or skilled persons, surgical facilities and 
life-saving drugs for handling emergency cases; and 
(c) if not, whether Government propose to take active help to NGOs in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) As per estimates provided by 
Registrar General of India through their Sample Registration System for 
1998; 407 Indian women die due to causes related to pregnancy & childbirth 
for every 100,000 live births. The World Health Organization estimates for 
1999, suggest that globally 600,000 women die every year due to these 
causes. 
(b) Under the Primary Health Care system, one Primary Health Centre 
(PHC) is established for 30,000 Population in plains and 20,000 population in 
hilly and tribal areas. Each PHC is manned by a qualified Medical Officer. 
Further, a Community Health Centre (CHC) is established for 1,20,000 
population in plains and 80,000 population in hilly and tribal areas. Each CHC 
has a sanctioned strength of 4 medical Specialists i.e. a physician, a surgeon, a 
Gynecologist & obstetrician and a Paediatrician. Each CHC has 30 beds, a 
labour room, and an operation theatre equipped with essential equipments. 
Essentially and Emergency Obstetric Care drug kits are supplied to the 
districts under the RCH Programme for use at identified PHCs and FRUs. 
(c)The National Population Policy, 2000 lists partnership with NGOs as 
one of the strategic themes. The work of NGOs is essentially supplementary 
and complementary in nature to that of the Government. Initially the NGOs were 
involved Imostly on activities related to advocacy and awareness creation in the 
community. NGOs are now being involved in providing services for maternal 
and child health care, family planning services, adolescent reproductive health, 
prevention and management of RTI and also in social marketing of 
contraceptives. Given that the NGOs have comparative advantage and 
flexibility in procedures, rapport with the local population and credibility, they 
are being involved in facilitating innovative approaches and strategies for 
ensuring accessibility to integrated health services and achievement of RCH 
Goals.

Fixation of prices of Medicines 
778. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: W ill the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the guidelines/yardsticks prescrib ed for fixation of prices of 
medicines; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the drug manufacturing companies are 
charging exorbitant prices for pills and drugs; 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take against such companies; 
and 
(d) the steps proposed to provide medicines at reasonable price? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a ) to (d) Prices of scheduled bulk 
drugs and formulations based there on are fixed/revised by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA)  in accordance with  the provisions 
of the Drugs Price Control Order (DPCO), 1995. Prices of Non Scheduled 
formulations are fixed by the manufacturers themselves keeping in view the 
various factors like cost of production, marketing/ selling expenses, R&D 
expenses, trade commission, market competition, product innovation, product 
quality etc. The Government takes corrective measures where the public interest 
is found to be adversely affected. Moreover, the drugs policy, as amended 
from time to time, is directed towards ensuring abundant availability of 
quality drugs at reasonable prices.

universal health insurance scheme has been designed in which the 
Government would contribute Rs. 100 per year towards the annual premium,

poverty line.

investment to 2% of GDP by the year 2010 from the existing level of 0.9%.

expenditure on health sector to 7% of their total budget by 2005 and to 8% of

per policy, subject to the overall    financial constraints.

Sale of spurious drugs 
793. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that fake and spurious drugs 
are ineffective against diseases and are a threat to health of human beings; 
(b) if so, the steps Government have taken to crack down on the 
manufactures of spurious drugs; 
(c) whether the High Court of Delhi has recently asked a report on 
circulation of spurious drugs in the country; and 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2003] 
(d) if so, the details of the report sent to the Delhi High Court? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND  
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Under the provisions of Drugs & Cosmetics act, 1940 and Rules 
thereunder, the responsibility for regulating manufacture and sale of drugs 
including monitoring their quality is vested with the state Governments. The 
State Governments are advised from time to time to gear up their enforcement 
machinery to detect and unearth spurious/ fake drugs moving in the inter-state 
commerce as well as to provide and strengthen their regulatory infrastructure to 
establish their own State level testing labs, to ensure speedy analysis of drug 
samples for which they are provided assistance to strengthen and augment 
their infrastructure facilities in their lab. The State Governments have also 
been advised to keep strict surveillance over the suspected dealers; collection 
of survey samples under National Su rvey Quality Eval uation of Drugs 
(NSQED) programme; c onstitution/reactivation of State drug advisory 
committees in which various trade and industry association as well as 
consumer associations can file representations; establishment of separate 
intelligence-cum-legal cell; to develop efficient communication facilities and 
recall procedures; engaging experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug 
cases etc. 
Government of India has taken the following initiatives to tackle the 
problem of spurious drugs:— 
(i) Detailed guidelines in respect of strategies required to be adopted for 
efficient surveillance over the movement of spurious drugs were given 
to States on November 17, 1999 to  ensure focused surveillance over 
manufacture and sale of spurious drugs. 
(ii) Issues concerning alleged sale of spurious drugs was taken up by 
Union Helath Minister with State Health Ministers in the 7th 
Conference of Central Council of Health (CCH) & FW held on 12-13 
July, 2001. CCH resolved that in order to address issues relating to the 
increasing reports of spurious drugs/counterfeit drugs, special 
attention requires to be given to monitor and unearth such illegal 
activities by constituting a separate 
140 

[28 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
intelligence-cum-legal cell in the respective drug control organization 
and in seeking cooperation of the pharma industry, trade as well as the 
police. 
(in) Department of Health constit uted a broad based Committee under the 
chairmanship of DGHS in July 2001 to examine issues concerning the 
problem of spurious durgs. The observations and recommendations of 
this Committee have been circulated on Sept. 16, 2002 to all State 
Drugs Controllers for their information and necessary action in the 
matter. 
(iv) Union Minister of Health & Family Welfare had specifically written to 
all Chief Ministers on Oct. 8, 2002 on the issue of spurious drugs, 
seeking their personal intervention to ensure that adequate measures are 
taken in each State to vigorously pursue the strategies needed to 
preclude any possibility of meanace of spurious products so as to 
collectively ensure its total eradication. 
(v) A meeting of Health Ministers and Senior Officials of 13 major States 
of the country was convened by Union Minister of Health & Family 
Welfare on 12.11.2002 to ensure  concerted action to check any 
possible movement of spurious drugs in the country and to involve all 
stakeholders to fight this meance. Suggestions/ views which emerged 
out of discussion were forwarded on  Jan. 8, 2003 to all the State 
Governments for their information and necessary action. One of the 
recommendations which emerged as outcome of discussion, was 
enactment of "The Gujarat Prevention of Anti-social Activities Act, 
1985" PASA by State Governments for deterrent action against 
offenders. 
(vi) In order to increase the number of drug samples tested in the country 
and to bring down the reporting time to less than a month as against 3 to 
6 months presently being taken by many laboratories, a 
comprehensive plan has been undertaken by Central Government 
under a capacity building project to be implemented with World Bank 
assistance. 
(vii) In order to ensure speedy information exchange and networking of all 
States and Central Drugs Contro l Offices and Laboratories, a 
computerization project has been undertaken by Central Government 
141 

RAJYA  SABHA [28 July, 2003] 
(viii) A Specialized training programme for drugs control officers of all 
State Governments responsible for keeping surveillance over possible 
movement of spurious drugs has been formulated and was conducted 
from 25 June. 2003 by Central Governments in cooperation with 
FDA, Maharashtra at Mumbai. 
(ix) Government of India have constituted a Committee of experts on 
January 27,2003 under the Chairmanship of Dr. R.A Mashelkar, 
Director General Council for Scie ntific and Industrial Research 
(CSIR) to undertake a comprehensiv e review of the drugs regulatory 
system in the country including the problem of spurious and 
substandard drugs and recommend remedial measures to deal with this 
problem effectively. The Committee has held two meetings on 
26.2.2003 and 17.7.2003 to undertake focused examination of two 
distinct areas of its terms of reference. Consultations with number of 
eminent persons and stakeholders has also been undertaken. One of 
the issues to be addressed by this committee is to introduce highly 
stringent and deterrent punishment for drug offenders. 
(c) and (d) Common Cause (Registered) Society filed a PIL (CWP No. 
8105/2002) in the High Court of Delhi, seeking intervention of the court to 
stop trading in spurious drugs in the Capital and asking the respondents 
(Government of Delhi and Government of India) to take measures to stop 
production, distribution, sale and possession of spurious drugs in the interest 
of general public. The Hoh'ble High Court heard the petitioner and 
respondents on 3.2.2003 and 1.4.2003 and passed interim order wherein the 
court directed Government of India, Mi nistry of Health and F.W. to place 
before the court by the end of Aug, 2003, a copy of the report, together with 
its gist, of the Expert Committee constituted by the Government of India 
under the chairmanship of Dr. R.A Ma helkar, DG, CSIR and Secretary to 
Government of India which is looking into the various issues related to drugs 
control administration including the matter of effectively tackling the problem 
of spurious drugs. The report of the Mashelkar Committee will be placed 
before the Court as and when it is made available.

been constantly reviewing the accumul ation of arrears in courts. Besides

Government have encouraged alternative modes of dispute resolution including 
conciliation, mediation and arbitration. Special tri bunals like Central 
Administrative Tribunal, State Admi nistrative Tribunals, Income Tax 
Appellate Tribunal, Labour Courts, Consumer Courts etc., have been set up

generation of causelists, providing information to the litigants/advocates etc.,

Adalats are being set up for expeditious resolution of disputes relating to public 
utilities.

for the use of information technology in the High Courts. Fast Track Courts 
have been set up to speed up the trial of delayed cases, and in particular the 
cases of undertrials who have been in jail for a long time.

vacant posts of Judges/Magistrates and supporting staff in District/ Subordinate

Ministry for the welfare of the persons with disabilities. There are six 
National Institutes/Apex level Institutio ns set up in each major area of 
disability which work, inter-alia, towards manpower development through 
long and short term training programmes, provide rehabilitation services, 
undertake functional research etc. The Artificial Limbs Manufacturing 
Corporation of India (ALIMCO), a public  sector undertaking under the aegis 
of this Ministry, manufactures and promotes the availability, supply and 
distribution of quality aids and appliances for persons with disabilities. The 
National Handicapped Finance and Development Corporation (NHFDC) 
provides financial assistance to persons with disabilities on soft terms, for 
self-employment and income generating activities. There is a scheme to 
provide support to non-government organization running various projects for 
rehabilitation of persons with disabilities. 
The Government has also taken initiatives to ensure wider coverage and 
holistic rehabilitation of persons with disabilities. Over a hundred districts 
have been identified for setting up District Centres with the objective of 
providing comprehensive rehabilitation services. Schemes are also under 
implementation for setting up Composite Regional Centres for providing 
composite rehabilitation services, and Regional Rehabilitation Centres 
(RRCs) for persons with spinal injuries and other orthopaedic disabilities. 
Besides, the National Programme for Rehabilitation of Persons with 
Disabilities (NPRPD) scheme has been approved in the State sector for 
creating infrastructure at the State/District/ Block and Gram Panchayat level 
for providing comprehensive rehabilitation services. The National Trust for 
Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cere bral Palsy, Mental Retardation and 
Multiple Disabilities has become functional. During the year 2002-03, an 
amount of Rs. 224.37 crores has been released under various schemes being 
implemented by the Ministry for the welfare of persons with disabilities.

Employment for disabled persons 
843. SHRI ABHAY KANT PRASAD: Will the Minister of SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have issued any orders to various 
Ministries/Departmental agencies to give priority in employment to the 
disabled; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the details of the action taken by Government in Jammu and 
Kashmir as compared to the other States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRI NAGMANI): (a) and (b) The 
Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995 provides for 3% reservation in 
employment in the establishment of Government of India and Public Sector 
Undertakings against posts identified as suitable for persons with Disabilities. 
The Government has notified a revised list of posts identified for Persons 
with Disabilities in the establishments of Government of India and Public 
Sector Undertakings in June, 2001. All Central Ministries/Departments have 
been requested by Department of Personnel and Training that while sending 
the requisitions for filling up of posts, which have been identified as suitable 
for appointment of persons with disabilities, a certificate should be given to 
the recruiting agencies that the policy relating to 3% reservation for persons 
with disabilities has been taken care of Ministry of Social Justice & 
Empowerment has also addressed State Governments regarding recruitment of 
persons with disabilities in government jobs to the extent of 3% of identified 
posts. 
(c) As per reports received from Stat e Commissioners for Persons with 
Disabilities, a provisions of minimum 3% reservation in employment for persons 
with disabilities has been made in 26 States/Union Territories. The Government 
of Jammu and Kashmir has its own law viz Jammu and Kashmir Persons with 
Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) 
Act, which came into force in 1998. This Act also provides for 3% 
reservation in employment for persons with disabilities.

859. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA : Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Comptroller and Auditor General of India has in his 
report pointed out serious lapses including violation of its bye-laws in 
connection with the allotment of residential units in the Narela Housing 
Scheme resulting in huge losses and blockage of funds amounting of Rs. 
36.08 crores;

DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) and (b) The Comptroller and Auditor General of 
India, in its report has pointed out that DDA constructed 6039 houses in the 
Narela Housing Scheme for various categories between December, 1993 to 
July, 1998 involving an expenditure of Rs. 115.39 crore. Due to non-
availability of the basic amenities like water supply and electricity, the 
scheme became unpopular resulting in re quest by allottees for cancellation of 
allotment of houses. Out of 6039 houses constructed 2003 houses remained 
unallotted after cancellation leading to the blockade of funds of Rs. 36.08 crore 
besides defeating the objective of providing housing to the public. 
(c) and (d) DDA has reported that some project related bottlenecks do 
take place in development of large sub-c ity like Narela inspite of assurances 
from various departments/organizations. However, though basic amenities 
like water and electricity were not available at the initial stage, this is not the 
sole or even the major reason for non-acceptance of the flats by the allottees. 
These facilities are now available in the area, but even then, many of the 
allottees are still not accepting the

will have to get the lease deed forms stamped before handing over

THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN : Now, we will have discussion on the 
Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Bill, 2003. Shri Jaswant Singh. 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI JASWANT SINGH) : Madam, I 
move that the Bill to provide for the re sponsibility of the Central Government 
to. ensure inter-generational equity in fiscal management and long-term 
macro-economic stability by achieving sufficient revenue surplus and removing 
fiscal impediments in the effective cond uct of monetary policy and prudential 
debt management consistent with fisca l sustainability through limits on the 
Central Government borrowings, debt a nd deficits, greater transparency in 
fiscal operations of the Central Government and conducting fiscal   policy  in   
a  medium-term   framework  and   for  matters  connected 
276 

[28 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
therewith or incidental thereto,  as passed by Lok Sabha,  be taken  into 
consideration. 
The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Bill, 2003 was 
introduced in the Parliament in December 2000 -- so, it has been a child of the 
Parliament for a very long time -- and was then, referred to the Standing 
Committee on Finance. After a detailed examination of the Bill, the Standing 
Committee, in its report, made various observations and recommendations. 
These were placed on the Table of the House in November, 2001. Based 
upon these recommendations, certain amendments in the Bill were carried 
out, and this Bill, along with all the proposed amendments, was passed by the 
Lok Sabha on the 7 th of May, 2003; thereafter, it reached the other House. 
Before the provisions in the Bill and amendments thereon are taken up for 
consideration, very briefly, Madam, I would request the hon. Members to 
reflect on the achievements of our economy. The decade of the 1990s has 
witnessed robust economic growth. It has been marked by benign inflation, 
steady growth in foreign exchange rese rves and a positive balance in current 
account. Whilst the macro economic parameters have been sound, there is an 
area that continues to cause concern,  and this pertains to sound fiscal 
management. The Central Government's high revenue and fiscal deficits 
necessitate enhanced borrowings, and you would appreciate, Madam, that I 
am not here going into the finances of  the State Governments, which we had 
occasion to discuss in a particular committee recently. The Central 
Government's high revenues and fiscal deficit necessitate enhanced 
borrowings, which in turn, add to the accretion of debt, and, in consequence, a 
higher cost of services. I may share with the hon. Members that the 
outstanding liabilities of the Central Government have risen steadily over the 
years, and as on March 31 st , 2004, the total liabilities are estimated to be 
around Rs. Eighteen lakh crores. The interest burden on these liabilities 
currently stands at Rs. one lakh twenty three thousand crores, thus pre-
empting almost half of our revenue receip ts. This is not tenable; this is also 
not sustainable. We need, obviously, to break free of this cycle of high deficit - 
high debt and we have to work, all of us, steadily, towards a regime of 
surpluses. If we had been able to transform a regime and an economy of 
deficit in food-grains, in the manufacturi ng industry, in services, and in other 
aspects of our national economy, ther e is no reason whatsoever, why we 
should not address ourselves to this very important aspect, and move 
determinedly towards a regime of surpluses. That is why this legislation,  
Madam, is historic in the country's fiscal management.  It 
277 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2003] 
obliges the Central Government to ensure fiscal sustainability in the medium 
term by generating revenue surplus and bringing down debt stock as a ratio of 
the GDP. Based upon the recommendations of the Standing Committee on 
Finance, it has been decided t hat specific targets that were stipulated in the 
Bill will no more form a part of the legislation. They will, however, be included 
in the rules to be framed under the Act. And the Fiscal Responsibility and 
Budget Management Bill, 2003 would also  enjoin the Government to table the 
following statements along with budgets every year Medium-Term Fiscal Policy 
Statement, Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, and Macro-economic Framework 
Statement. This will place the budgeting exercise in a larger macro-economic 
framework and long-term perspective so as to ensure transparency, stability 
and consistency with long-term policy ob jective.   With these words, I 
commend the Bill to this august House.

per cent of the revenues are being pre- empted to meet the salaries, pensions 
and other establishment expenditure. Naturally, Governments have to borrow. 
But the most part of the fiscal defici t essentially represents the borrowings. 
Fiscal deficit is nothing but, in simple terms, borrowing that is being made. The

assets.    They are being

some figures that the hon. Finance Minister has given in the
